title: Making comparisons
goal: Compare two things and name the one that's the most — with two regular endings and a handful of irregular forms that happen to be the ones used most.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Stockholm eller Göteborg?
dialogs.intro: Dian is considering an internship in Göteborg. Oskar, who was born there, has plenty of opinions.

lines.text: Nej, Stockholm är mycket större. Men Göteborg är trevligare.

notes: **Än means "than"** and is never confused with *som*. *Större **än** Stockholm* (bigger than Stockholm), *lika stor **som** Stockholm* (as big as Stockholm). Two words for two different relationships — exactly like English *than* and *as*.

**Sämre** and **bäst** are the irregular forms of *dålig* and *bra*. The six most common adjectives have comparative forms that look nothing like the base word, and unfortunately there's no way round learning them. The good news: there are only six — and English has the very same habit (good, better, best; bad, worse, worst).

**Den regnigaste staden** — the "most" form in a definite phrase follows the double-definiteness rule from Unit 12: *den* in front, the ending *-en* on the noun, and an ending on the adjective. Superlatives in *-ast* take *-e* (*den regnigaste staden*), while the short *-st* ones take *-a* (*den största staden*, *det bästa sättet*). You may also hear *-e* for a male person: *den bäste läraren*. At A1, the *-a* form of *bäst*, *störst* and friends is right in almost every sentence.

**Tycka om** means "to like", and the particle is required: *jag tycker om kaffe*. Without *om*, *tycka* means "to think, to be of the opinion": *jag tycker att kaffe är gott*. Two very different meanings, separated by one little word.

**Dubbelt så hög** — "twice as high". The patterns *så … som* and *dubbelt så …* let you compare without any ending, just as in English: *lika dyr som* (as expensive as), *hälften så stor* (half as big), *tre gånger så många* (three times as many).
**Så klart** means "of course, obviously" — the casual cousin of *självklart*. Together with *absolut*, *precis* and *exakt*, these are the emphatic words you'll hear every day.

grammars.title: Two endings for comparing
after: The last two rows show a small group of adjectives that **change their vowel**: *stor → större → störst*, *ung → yngre → yngst*, *lång → längre → längst*, *hög → högre → högst*, *låg → lägre → lägst*, *tung → tyngre → tyngst*. They are all short, very common words — think of English *old → elder → eldest*.

**Long** adjectives — especially ones derived from other words — use *mer* and *mest* instead of an ending, just as English uses "more" and "most": *intressant → **mer** intressant → **mest** intressant*, *praktisk → mer praktisk → mest praktisk*. Rough rule: three syllables or more, use *mer/mest*.
The "more" form in *-are* **never changes** for gender or number: *en större bil*, *ett större hus*, *större bilar*. That saves you a whole layer of memorizing.

grammars.title: The irregular six
after: You already know the last two rows from Unit 5: *många* for things you can count, *mycket* for things you can't. Their comparatives keep the same distinction: *fler böcker* (more books), *mer kaffe* (more coffee) — the same line English draws between "fewer" and "less", or "many" and "much".

English has a very similar list, and some of the family resemblance shows: *bättre–better*, *bäst–best*, *mindre–less*, *äldre–elder*, *mer–more*, *mest–most*. Half this table is already half-learned.

blocks.text: Swedish keeps **tycka / tro / veta** strictly apart, and foreigners often blur them — English speakers especially, because English uses "I think" for both of the first two. *Tycker* is for taste and judgment ("I think the film is good"), *tror* is for a guess about a fact ("I think he's gone home"), *vet* is for what you actually know. Saying *jag tycker att han är hemma* sounds odd, because whether someone is at home isn't a matter of opinion.

blocks.title: Comparing without an ending
items: **lika … som** — as … as: *Göteborg är lika trevligt som Malmö.*
**inte lika … som** — not as … as: *Bussen är inte lika snabb som tåget.*
**dubbelt så …** — twice as…: *Hyran är dubbelt så hög.*
**ju … desto …** — the more … the more…: *Ju längre norrut, desto kallare.*
**allt** + "more" form — more and more…: *Det blir allt kallare.*

blocks.text: **Göteborg** is pronounced **yö-teh-BORY** — the first *g* becomes a *y* sound because it stands before *ö*, and the *-borg* at the end melts into *bory*, with a quick y-glide. (In English the city is often called Gothenburg; in Swedish, only Göteborg will do.) It's one of the names newcomers get wrong most often, and locals notice immediately when you say it right.
